paragraphs: Walsall Council runs a not-for-profit fostering service, rated good by Ofsted, from Fallings Heath in Darlaston. It says it always tries to match children with its own foster carers first, before looking to independent agencies such as the services shown above. The council is also one of four, with Dudley, Sandwell and Wolverhampton, behind Black Country Fostering, a shared partnership that gives people one point of contact for information and advice, alongside training for existing carers.

The council's placement sufficiency strategy for 2025 to 2028 counted 578 children in its care on 31 March 2025, down from 665 a year earlier, and by the end of June 2025, 71.4% of them were living in foster care. Children aged 10 and over now make up 59% of those in care, and the strategy names older boys with more complex needs as a growing group. One of its priorities is for more children to live in or near Walsall, connected to their communities.

That shapes what the council asks of carers. Its emergency scheme takes young people, usually aged 10 to 18, at short notice, and it offers short breaks for young people with disabilities or complex needs. New Horizon finds family homes for children, usually aged 10 to 18, who are living in children's homes; it asks for at least two years' experience with young people whose behaviour can be challenging and one carer based at home.

From April 2026 Walsall pays a weekly household fee and an allowance for each child. The fee for one child is £246, or £307 for advanced carers, and New Horizon Mockingbird carers receive £900. Child allowances run from £182 a week for under-fives to £267 for those aged 16 and over, with an extra week at birthdays and festivals and two weeks in the summer holidays. Carers in the borough pay no council tax to Walsall, and those living outside it get an equivalent payment. Our Walsall allowance page has the full table.

Walsall was the first council in the West Midlands to adopt Mockingbird, launched in July 2018, and now runs six constellations in which a hub carer supports a group of fostering families. New carers also get a buddy, coffee mornings and out-of-hours help. Compare the council with two or three of the services above, and see our pages for Wolverhampton, Dudley, Sandwell and the West Midlands.
